who: Tian et al. 2024, 'Are LLMs capable of storytelling' (alphaxiv overview read, not the paper)
claim: GPT-4 synopses: >51% 'Man in a Hole' vs 30.7% human; downbeat arcs (Riches to Rags, Oedipus) nearly absent; valence rises steadily; major setback and climax placed earlier (premature resolution); less suspense/arousal in middle-to-end. Turning-point planning lifted 'best for suspense' to 48.3% vs 7.9% outline-only. Models hit requested negative arcs <55% of the time.
relevance: Direct: LLM default is rising valence and early resolution. A per-beat valence/turn field lets code see the drift; plan turning points explicitly, and check the model obeyed a requested down-turn.

claim: Gate story steps behind accumulated resources ('pacing wheels'); show players how far they are from what they are reaching for; repeatable filler must be short, generic and offer choices or it goes stale.
relevance: Ashfall's beats unlock on game state = pacing wheels. Check every beat has a visible 'reaching for' goal; repeatable runtime lines short.

claim: Content needs at least two interacting qualities or it 'risks becoming a simplistic chain or a grind'; make characters tangible through visible consequences (menaces like Wounds); don't stack many quality changes in one result or each matters less; design for players returning after breaks (reminders).
relevance: Flag beats whose unlock depends on a single counter (chain/grind); each costly beat names one visible consequence, not five; recap hooks for short-session returners.

claim: Free-floating repeatable storylets lack momentum; quality-gated chains ('questicles') add 'a beginning, a middle and an end'; one-time content ('Mark of Cain') gives finality because once done 'it's gone forever'.
relevance: Each beat should belong to a thread with a start/middle/end; flag orphan beats not part of any thread.

claim: QBN risks: author tracks progression by hand; players lose the chain of causality; salience can sequence into undramatic orders. Remedies: weight selection by dramatic-arc considerations; 'run a few thousand randomized playthroughs and use some visualization tools' to find unused or overused sequences.
relevance: Ashfall already simulates sharp/typical/lazy players; extend the sim to emit beat order per route and run the flatness checks on each route, not just the authored order.

who: arXiv 2402.17119 (authors not read), 2024, 'Creating Suspenseful Stories: Iterative Planning with LLMs' (abstract only)
claim: Zero-shot iterative planning grounded in suspense theory from cognitive psychology/narratology beat baseline on suspense in human evaluation; abstract gives no n.
relevance: Plan-level: a beat outline should name what the protagonist/town is trying and what threatens it; critique at the plan, not the prose. The 'plan vs obstacle' mechanism is my reading of suspense theory, not stated in the abstract.

who: Greg Kasavin (Supergiant), via GeekDad/ScreenHub/Game Developer interviews (search snippets only)
claim: Hades' variety is 'around the game state': characters talk about specific things depending on the exact moment; story advances a little on every death; bosses/characters remember prior encounters.
relevance: Short sessions: every visit should carry at least one state-specific line referencing what just happened; check runtime prompts receive a recent-event fact.

who: Brandon Sanderson (BYU lectures; secondary summaries only)
claim: Plot = promises, progress, payoff; a middle without visible progress on a promise reads as 'going nowhere'; payoffs must answer promises made.
relevance: Promise ledger: each beat opens/progresses/pays ids; flag a week with no progress on any open promise, and promises never paid.

who: TV commentary (Jed Hartman; Fringe critique on PopMatters; TV Tropes 'Half-Arc Season'), not writers' rooms
claim: Standalone episodes sag when 'nothing really happens' to the main characters; long premises stretched over many episodes recycle dynamics; half-arc seasons front- and back-load the arc. Most-cited fix: character continuity so viewers feel progress even in standalones.
relevance: Mini-stories between spine beats should still move a recurring character (state change on a named person); flag mini-stories that change no one.

who: Robert McKee, Story (via McKee blog snippet and reader notes; book text not read)
claim: A scene turns a value-charged condition from positive to negative or the reverse; if the value is the same at the end as the start, the scene is a 'nonevent' however much activity it has.
relevance: Per-beat 'value' and 'turn' fields; flag beats with no turn and runs of same-direction turns.

who: Sanderson; Mary Robinette Kowal (attributed); John D. Brown 'Plot Basics' (summaries)
claim: Try-fail cycles escalate: 'yes, but' (success with complication) and 'no, and' (failure, worse); a clean 'yes' stops the story.
relevance: Outcome field yes|yes_but|no|no_and per attempt-beat; flag long runs of clean 'yes' (LLM tidy-resolution bias).

who: Chakrabarty et al., 'Art or Artifice?' CHI 2024 (abstract + search snippet on TTCW dimensions)
claim: LLM stories passed 3-10x fewer of 14 TTCW tests than professional stories (10 expert raters, 48 stories); TTCW includes Narrative Pacing and Scene vs Exposition; 'none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments' as judges.
relevance: Blind LLM critics are unreliable at holistic quality; restrict them to narrow, near-binary structural questions with a quoted span as evidence, and keep holistic judgement for a human.

who: Wikipedia; PocketGamer (Amir Rajan, attribution unclear); Medium essay (search snippets only)
claim: A Dark Room tells its story almost entirely through environmental cues and restraint; players report the story, not the tapping, hooked them. No primary designer source found on where idle-game stories thin.
relevance: Null on 'where idle stories thinned' beyond the owner's own Cookie Clicker report in decisions.md. Supports system-carried story; not a check.
